title: Studies in the Ramayana: the Geography and Ethnology of the Poem
html:
STUDIES
IN THE RAMAYANA.

BY

Mr. C. TIRUMALAYYA NAIDU, M. R. A. S.

THE GEOGRAPHY AND ETHNOLOGY OF THE POEM.

A knowledge of geography and an ethnological survey of the country comprised in the Ramayana will be found to be necessary for an elucidation of many an intricate situation occurring in the poem. In the words of Mr. Cust, 'the glimpses of geographical knowledge afore-said of the poet are highly interesting to trace out; and the insight gained into the habits and manners of the people at the time the poem was written is invaluable.' The geography of the poem may not always be credible: but it is interesting as showing the extent and accuracy of the knowledge possessed by the poet. It is curious to find that, though the whole continent of what is now known as India was roughly known to the poet, he nowhere refers to it as a single whole, nor does he give any separate name for it. The name India is said to be derived from the Greek and the Roman adaptation of the word Hindu, which was used by the Persians for their Aryan brethren, because the latter settled in the districts surrounding the streams of the Sindhi (pronounced by them Hindu and now called Indus). The words Bharatavarsha and Aryavarta do not occur in the poem. The latter was the name given by Manu to the region between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains. Bharata was the most famous ruler of the Lunar dynasty and reigned at Hastinapura, the modern Delhi, over a more or less large part of India, which was henceforth known after his name.

The poem opens with a description of the Kosala country on the bank of the Sarayu, the modern Gogra, which is supposed to have had its origin in the lake Manasaras, in the Himalayas. Although Ayodhya, its capital, whose extent was twelve yojanas in length and three in breadth (a yojana varying from four to eight miles) was 'the base of operations in the story, still the poet takes us through a vast extent of country, conducting us now beyond the Sutlej into the Panjab, now across the Vindhya mountains into the Dekhan, and now across the Narmada and Godavari to the most southern parts of India, even to the island of Ceylon.' Ikshwaku was its first king, and ruled over a large territory of land, which was known as 'Ikshwaku's dominions,' under which name Rama conveniently includes the country known as Kishkindha and ruled by Vali (Vide Kishkindha Kânda, Sarga 18 and Sloka 6). Though Daçaratha boasted to Kaikeyi that his dominions extended as far as 'the wheel of the sun' could go, still he explicitly referred to countries like Sindhu, Savari, Sourashtra, Dakshinapatha, Vanga, Anga, Maghadha, Matsya, Kasi, and Kosala, over which he claimed a sort of suzerainty, from which he offered to get whatever she might be inclined to command! (Ayodhya Kânda, Sarga X, Sloka 37). But we know that Anga was ruled by Romapada, whom he mentions as his friend. But the invitations which Daçaratha issued on the occasion of his great horse sacrifice were confined to the rulers of Mithila, Kasi, Kêkaya, Anga, Sindhu, Savari and Sourashtra, and to many other nameless kings (Bala Kânda, Sarga XIII, Slokas 21 to 25). The poet's knowledge of this part of the country namely, the region to the north of the Vindhya, is more or less complete and the description of the whole country as detailed by Viswamithra to Rama on their way to Mithila is wonderfully minute. But beyond this, there was the great Dandaka forest infested with deadly reptiles and ferocious beasts of prey, and inhabited by cannibalistic Rakshasas. On the other side of the Sarayu, lived the tribe of the Nishadas, a race of pygmies, whose ruler was Guha and whose capital was Sringibera.

An unbiassed study of the poem cannot but convince the reader that the great and perpetual struggle between the Rishis and the Rakshasas was the result of the aggressive colonization by the former, of the territories which were already under the unquestioned occupation of the latter. The great alluvial plains of the south, and the splendid possibilities of colonization in the continuous and beautiful forest with its myriads of flowering plants and fruit trees, and abounding in all sorts of wild game, and with its flowing rivers full of lotuses and lilies and of many varieties of edible fish, very early attracted the Rishis who founded amidst unceasing opposition, many hermitages which were innocently so called but which were really bases of operation against the accredited inhabitants of the plains. What was known as the Siddhasrama, originally belonged to the Emperor Bali, probably a very early ruler of the place who was, by inexcusable cunning and under the pretence of mendicancy, subjugated by Vishnu in the guise of a dwarf. Thus probably arose the feuds between the subjects of Bali and these aggressive colonists. Viswamitra whose permanent abode was on the bank of the Kowsi in the Himalayas makes it convenient to come down to the place for performing a sacrifice, although nothing prevented him from doing the same in his own asrama and in a more peaceful manner befitting his religious order. The Rakshasas naturally represented this unjustifiable intrusion, which necessitated his applying to Daçaratha for help. Many such hermitages were already founded and were known by the names of those Rishis who, more boldly than others, took to adventures of this kind. These were known as Bharadwaju Asrama, Sarabhanga Asrama, Atri Asrama, Sutikishna Asrama, Matanga Asrama, Agastya Asrama, &c. Beyond these Asramas, there was Janastana, the modern Naśik, which was probably the northern confines of Ravana's realm, where was quartered a large contingent of his army, headed by his own brothers Khara and Dusana, with a view apparently to keep watch over the determined incursions of the Rishis, and of their docile warrior rulers who were only too ready to carry out whatever they were bidden to do by the Rishis. The Ramayana is nothing but the history of the attempted colonization of a strange country by the Rishis and of the feuds which these bold incursions naturally gave rise to. Far down in the south, on the banks of the Pamoâ lake, there was the principality of Kishkindha, of which Vâli was the ruler.

An attempt was made by the poet to put in the mouth of Sugriva a description of the early geography of the world, which is, however, most unreliable, owing to its hopeless exaggerations. But it is interesting to find mention thereof Cheena (China) in the north, which probably supplied, from the earliest times, the best silks, which formed the chief raiment of the aristocratic classes. But more trust-worthy is the description of the countries near the Godavery, and the Andhra, Pundra, Chola, Pandya and Kerala kingdoms in the south, where grew the stately cocoa-nut and sandal-wood trees in luxurious abundance. The banks of the Kaveri and Tambraparni are also referred to as the places where the search party headed by Angada and Hanuman sojourned for a time before they found a clue to the island of Lanka.

Far more instructive is the study of the characteristics of the races of men that came in contact with each other in the course of the story. Broadly speaking, there were the Kshatriya race of the Solar descent, with their family preceptors the Rishis (who were not all Brahmins), the Nishadas, the Vanaras of the Central India, and the so-called Rakshasas who perpetually collided with their militant brethren of the North. The hero of the poem belonged to the Solar race whose origin is traced from Brahma through the Sun-god. But, for all practical purposes, Ikshwaku was the great ancestor who founded the dynasty known after his name. This race was characterised by all those qualities of the head and heart which go to make a great nation. A great line of worthy rulers, their rule was characterised by wise statesmanship and righteous conduct, which endeared them to their subjects. 'But the Rishis who were their family priests, and secular advisers as well, early succeeded in encouraging the growth of a sort of superstitious awe for, and in fostering an ever-increasing and servile dependence on, themselves for good and evil alike. The superstitious rulers feared their wrath, though heroic by nature and wise by culture. The Rishis, on their part, showed an inordinate zeal and anxious concern for their welfare and fame. In fact, the solar race owed its glorious successes as well as its ignominious failures to the machinations of these learned men. So far as internal economy was concerned, the Rishis, it must be said to their credit, were eminent for their impartiality, fair-mindedness and justice which was evenly administered between man and man. But, in the management of 'foreign affairs,' they hopelessly lacked that equitableness and fairness which alone secured peace. It was the Rishis that developed the plot which ultimately brought Rama into violent contact with the Rakshasas. When the latter requested their help in finding for him a suitable place in the forest where he could conveniently bide his time during the period of his self-exile, they strategically took him from place to place, till they pointed out Janastana as the best residential quarter for him. He did not know that it was a place thickly populated by the fierce-looking Rakshasas, till he met Sūrpanakha in one of her aimless wanderings. He was looked upon by her with suspicion which soon changed into fierce lust provoked by his handsome person. This part of the story is too well-known to need any recapitulation here. After the obstruction of the whole army of the Rakshasas, the Rishis approached him highly elated at his success and informed him with unconcealed satisfaction that he was most cunningly lured on to this place by them for the purpose of exterminating the cruel and sinful Rakshasas: (Vide Aranya Kanda, Sarga XXX and Sloka 31) Rama only too fully realized this, after Sita was taken from him. (Aranya Kanda, Sarga 57, Sloka 9.) They, while jealous of their own possessions, were victim to that 'earth hunger' which really proved a bar to an otherwise just rule. The Nishadas were an insignificant people who played a very minor part in the development of the story.

The Monkey-tribes, known as the Vânaras, occupied the central plateau of India and were conspicuous for their valour. Their colonies seem to have extended far and wide. Modern research has shown that they belonged to the Kolarian race, which probably represents the earliest settlers in India, whose country was later on encroached upon by the Dravidian races, who were sometimes friendly and sometimes inimical to them. Their stage of civilization could be inferred by the knowledge of the arts displayed by them as described by the poet. It was perhaps their dark and ugly features, smallness of stature, flattened nose, hairy growth and predatory habits, and their occupation of jungly and marshy tracts, shunning the haunts of men that had brought upon them the contempt of their fellow-beings. The Rakshasas are represented as the most hated of the Rishis whom they were not tired of molesting. But the poet showed no prejudice in delineating their characteristics. He displays true historical insight when he depicted them as belonging to a civilization which was in no way inferior to that of the Solar race itself. Occasional relapses into hyperbolical digressions on the part of the poet, such as the representation of the three-headed Trisiras, the ten-headed Ravana, the ever-sleepy Kumbakarna, the hideous Surpanakha, were probably intended to excite the flagging interest of the varied readers of this ponderous work with its inevitable repetitions. In the same way, in describing races unknown to the Greeks, such as the Cyclopes, Laestrogones, Centouræ, &c., Homer and other Greek writers are given to exaggeration and relate the most absurd tales. But the Rakshasas seem to have been an enlightened race, whose pugnacity and vindictiveness were due to the provocative depredations of the later Aryan settlers, but who were peaceful citizens in their own country, when left to themselves unmolested and unharassed. (Aranya Kanda, Sarga XXXVIII, Sloka 24). When Sita heard that Rama had peldged himself at any cost to protect the Rishis from the molestations of the Rakshasas, she very rightly tried her best to dissuade him from undertaking hostilities on their behalf, for which he could plead no sort of justification. She tells him that “an attempt to fight others unprovoked, is one of the three afflictions which man brings on himself by his own wantonness. I do not like the very idea of your entering the forest inhabited by the Rakshasas. I do not like that lives should be sacrificed without any cause for provocation. It is incumbent on you to practise the duty prescribed for those who have vowed to spend their lives in peaceful contemplation. You will please my father-in-law and mother-in-law by following such a duty.” (Aranya Kanda, Sarga IX, Slokas 3½ to 32½.) A very sound advice which Rama, however, preferred not to follow because of the promise he had already made to them, without any forethought of the consequences of such an action. In Lanka some of the Rakshasas were very handsome, wise, learned in arts and skilled in Vedic lore. But for his blind and unquenchable lust, Ravana was himself great not only by his vast learning and erudition but also by his tremendous valour and intrepidity which he displayed fearless of its after-results, and which provoked the admiration of his honest foes. There can be no doubt that these Rakshasas were the earliest Aryan settlers in India * which could be proved from the various Aryan customs and manners prevalent among them as described by Valmiki. It is very probable that as Monier Williams thinks, soon after their final occupation of the Gangetic districts, a body of invaders headed by a bold leader such as Ravana, might have forced their way far down into the south of India and into Ceylon. It was as mentioned above, the aggressive spirit of the later Aryan incursionists that was the cause of the conflict between the two branches of the same Aryan stock.

The Rakshasas—A Note.

Mr. C. Tirumalayya Naidu's statement that the Rakshasas were the earliest Aryan settlers in India and were a branch of one and the same Aryan stock, seems to be deduced from the fact of their customs and manners resembling those of the Aryans. But there are many points in the Ramayana itself which clearly assign to the Rakshasas a different nationality. They certainly differed from the Aryan invaders as to their origin, civilization and worship.

(1) We know that the Aryans were a white-coloured people; while the Rakshasas are invariably described as a black race. Here, however, the question may be raised that Rama, the hero of the Ramayana, is also described as a black man. This of course is an exceptional case. Besides, as I have elsewhere put it, the author of this popular Epic seems to have had before him an old story of the South which he has grafted upon the story of Rama of Kosala and completed the grand work. the Ramayana. The word Rama itself means "the black one" from the very old Tamilian root ir (Iṛ), "to be darkened." [Though the root is now lost, it survives in the following words: இரா (ira), "night"; இருள் (irul) "dark"; இருக்தை (irundai), "charcoal"; இருப்பு (irumbu), "black metal." (i. e. iron); and இராமன் (Raman), "blackman." The feminine of இராமன் (Raman) is இராமாயி (Ramayi) which we find generally used amomg the lower classes, as proper names.] To the oriental mind, the term 'black' is often associated in idea with beauty. So Raman conveys to the mind the idea of a black but fair man, just as the word காரிணை (Karikai) is suggestive of a "black, but fair woman," from the root கரு (Karu) "to blacken."

(2) From the Ramayana we learn that the Rakshasas were a highly civilized people. They had attained a high degree of civilization independently of the Aryans, nay, were even more civilized than the early Aryans. The position assigned to women in the Aryan community was comparatively inferior; among the Rakshasas women held an honourable position.

The ancient Dravidian lady was the mistress of the house and heiress and owner of all property, and she held the right to select her husband at her own choice, known as Swayamvaram. But among the Aryans, the marriage system was from very early times Kanyadhanam, "giving of the daughter", and heirship was patriarchal. From the Uttarakanda we learn that Ravana took possession of Lanka by maternal right, for heirship among ancient Dravidians was matriarchal and not as with the Aryan's patriarchal, a clear proof of their different nationality. (See my article on the "Pandavas and the Tamilian Kings", Tamilian Antiquary, No. 1, pp. 61—64).

(3) The differences in religion and in worship are also most striking. The Aryans were polytheists and worshippers of heavenly bodies. But the Rakshasas were monotheists and worshippers of Civa, the Supreme Lord of the Dravidas, not included in the Aryan pantheon. Besides, the Aryans were performers of Yágas, while their enemies were destroyers of such bloody sacrifices, which were intended to obtain only some material good. The Aryan worship of natural phenomena and their unmeaning sacrifices appeared to the philosophical Tamil mind to be sacrilegious. The Rakshasas as well as the Asuras of olden days—the ancestors of the Tamilian race,—worshipped their Supreme Lord, the God, Civa, in the form of a Linga, "emblem" or "image" with incense and flowers, and their ultimate aim was the attainment of heavenly bliss. [See my essays on the "Admixture of Aryan with Tamilian," in the pages of the Siddhanta Deepika, and the Educational Review, for years 1900—1901.]

These are the most striking differences between the two rival races. They show that they represented two different nationalities and that Ravana and his followers belonged to the Asuras or the ancient Tamilians. And I dare say that Mr. Griffith is right when he says: "The people against whom Rama waged war are different in origin, in civilization, and in worship." Though the name Rakshasa became hated, and contemptible in latter days, it was at first an honorific name and meant “the protectors,” equivalent to the Tamilian word ane or pyane which means “protectors of the country.” Even the proper names in the Epic are sanskritised by the poet as Ravana, Vibheeshana, Kumba-karna, &c. This cannot lead one to treat them as Aryans, for we see also the names of other peoples who were beyond doubt non-Aryan, sanskritised, as Sugriva, Hanuman, Jadayu, &c. Again, it is an acknowledged fact that the Dravidian ethnologically belongs to the Caucasian melanochroid physical type of the human species, a branch of Homo Caucasicus of Mr. Keane. Therefore, there is nothing strange in the remarks of our friend Mr. C.T. Naidu, viz., “In Lanka some of the Rakshasas were very handsome.”

If Monier Williams is of the same opinion as our friend Mr. Tirumalayya Naidu, who quotes him, I should say he is wrong. But the text from his “Indian Wisdom” which I beg to quote below, clearly shows that the Author’s view about the Rakshasas is different from that of Mr. Tirumalayya Naidu. “It is certainly likely,” says M. Williams, “ that at some early date, not long after the first settlement of the Aryan races in the country of the five rivers, rival tribes of immigrants, called Kurus, advancing from that region towards the plains of Hindustan, contended for supremacy. It is, moreover, probable that soon after their first occupation of the Gangetic districts, a body of invaders headed by a bold leader, and aided by the warlike but uncivilized hill-tribes, forced their way southwards unto the Peninsula of India as far as Ceylon. The heroic exploits of the chieftains in both cases would naturally become the theme of epic poetry, and the wild Aborigines of the Vindhya and neighbouring hills would be poetically converted into Monkeys, while the powerful Pre-aryan races of the south would be represented as many-headed ogres and blood-thirsty demons..... In the epic poems they are generally called Rakshasas or evil demons, the relentless enemies of Gods and good men and of all sacred rights.” (Indian Wisdom, p p. 311-313.)
